hints: Start in the centre of the small circular fibre and work outwards - look at the pale core in the middle and then the thick dark layered ring wrapped tightly around it.
Recall which type of glial cell wraps its cell surface membrane many times around the nerve fibre to make that dark insulating layer, and what the conducting core inside is called.
walkthrough:
Reading the Electron Micrograph**
Think of this as a slice straight across a cable. The pale area in the middle labelled B is the conducting wire itself, the axon with its cytoplasm called axoplasm. Around it you see many dark concentric lines like onion rings.

Linking Structure to the Wrapping Cell**
Those dark rings are many layers of cell surface membrane wrapped tightly around the axon. That wrapping is the myelin sheath, and it is made by a Schwann cell. So A is the Schwann cell / myelin sheath and B is the axon.
Final answer: A - Schwann cell / myelin sheath; B - axon / axoplasm.

hints: Picture a myelinated axon along its length - where are the small gaps in the myelin where the axon membrane is exposed?
Think about how depolarisation at one exposed gap sets up local currents in the cytoplasm and tissue fluid to the next gap.
Compare jumping a long distance between gaps with having to regenerate an action potential at every point, and link this to overall speed.
walkthrough:
Where Action Potentials Can Happen**
Myelin is an electrical insulator, so sodium and potassium channels and action potentials are concentrated at the gaps called nodes of Ranvier. Between nodes the membrane is insulated and cannot depolarise.

Jumping by Local Circuits**
When one node depolarises during an action potential, local circuits of ions flow between that depolarised node and the next resting node. This brings the next node to threshold quickly without needing to regenerate the action potential in the myelinated region.

Effect on Speed**
Because the impulse effectively jumps from node to node over longer distances, saltatory conduction greatly increases the speed of transmission along the neurone.
Final answer: Action potential jumps from node of Ranvier to node of Ranvier; longer local circuits / currents set up between nodes; increases speed of impulse transmission.

hints: Start the normal story at the presynaptic knob - what ions normally rush in when the action potential arrives, and what channels does the toxin block?
Think about what those ions normally do to the vesicles full of transmitter inside the presynaptic knob.
Follow the chain forward - if nothing is released by exocytosis, what is missing from the synaptic cleft?
Consider what normally happens on the postsynaptic membrane when transmitter binds to receptors, especially sodium channels.
Link failure of sodium entry and depolarisation to why threshold is never reached for a new action potential.
walkthrough:
Blocking the Calcium Trigger**
Normally an arriving action potential opens voltage-gated calcium ion channels and calcium ions flood into the presynaptic knob. Here the toxin blocks those channels, so no calcium ions enter.

No Vesicle Fusion and No ACh Release**
Calcium is the signal that makes vesicles containing acetylcholine, ACh, move to and fuse with the presynaptic membrane. Without calcium there is no exocytosis, so no ACh is released and none diffuses across the synaptic cleft.

No Postsynaptic Depolarisation**
With no ACh, there is no binding to ACh receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. That means chemically-gated sodium ion channels stay closed, sodium ions do not enter, and the postsynaptic membrane is not depolarised.

No New Action Potential**
An action potential in the postsynaptic neurone only starts if depolarisation reaches threshold. Since depolarisation never happens, no action potential is generated in the postsynaptic neurone.

Final answer: No Ca2+ entry into presynaptic knob, so vesicles do not fuse with presynaptic membrane and no exocytosis / release of ACh; no ACh diffusion across cleft and no binding to receptors on postsynaptic membrane; Na+ channels stay closed, no Na+ entry, no depolarisation, so no postsynaptic action potential.
